awd_titl_txt: CAREER: Neural Network-Inspired Information Processing Beyond the Binary Digital Abstraction
awd_abstract_narration:
This project approaches the question of higher performance and better energy efficiency in electronic chip design with two key insights from biological systems: non-Boolean information encoding (analog processing in brain), and co-localized memory and computation (as in brain synapses). The specific objective of this project is to create a design framework for efficient information processing with intrinsic non-binary representations and in-memory memory and computation. If successful, this project can shed light on the fundamental role of information encoding and its physical implementation in determining system energy efficiency, as well as provide practical design automation methodology to infuse computation and learning into the analog/mixed-signal (AMS) domain before the digitalization step. Apart from its technological impacts, the integrated educational plan of this project is to empower students from all backgrounds with interdisciplinary experience and to cultivate a community of lifelong learners with social awareness.

The project will enable joint optimization of circuit, architecture, and algorithm in a seamless manner across wide-range of applications including in-memory computing (IMC) and near-sensor processing (NSP), and consists of three major research thrusts: (1) to advance AMS design automation, novel neural network-inspired model abstraction, and hardware substrate will be developed to enable a streamlined design flow that uses AMS circuits as building blocks for information processing; (2) to support flexible and efficient in-memory computing architecture, this project will build intelligent and malleable peripheral interfaces and compilation framework by leveraging the AMS design methodology developed earlier; (3) to address the energy efficiency challenge in resource-constrained sensor systems, it will explore a context-aware analog-to-information frontend design by developing efficient near-sensor processing with multiple signal channels and multiple sensing modalities. These will serve as building blocks towards understanding the holistic interactions and design trade-offs of performance, efficiency, safety, and security in heterogeneous systems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report

Today's computers process information as strings of ones and zeros. This "binary digital abstraction" has powered decades of progress, but it is increasingly costly in energy, especially as artificial intelligence (AI) spreads into data centers, phones, cameras, and medical devices. The human brain, by contrast, processes rich sensory information on about 20 watts. It does so by representing information in continuous, non-binary forms and by computing where information is stored. This CAREER project asked how electronic systems could borrow these principles to become far more efficient. It also asked how AI itself could help engineers design the analog circuits that make this possible.

Intellectual Merit

The project pursued three connected research directions.

The first direction was neural network-inspired circuit design. We showed that neural networks can serve as blueprints for analog circuits. This line of work grew into a broader effort to use AI to automate analog circuit design, a task that has long depended on scarce human expertise. We developed methods that automatically tune circuit parameters and, more ambitiously, invent entirely new circuit structures. Our AnalogGenie family of models generates novel, valid circuit designs at scale. Our PowerGenie framework discovered a power converter design that outperforms both the designs it learned from and published human-engineered designs, while using much less chip area. Along the way, we created tools that predict a circuit's performance in seconds rather than hours. We also built benchmarks revealing that today's most capable AI models still struggle to reason about circuits mathematically.

The second direction was computing in and near memory. Moving data between memory and processors consumes much of the energy in modern computing. We designed memory systems that perform calculations directly inside memory, improving energy efficiency and speed by two to four times over prior designs. We also studied how such hardware can securely and economically serve large-scale recommendation systems in data centers.

The third direction was intelligent sensors. Cameras capture far more raw data than most applications need. We developed image sensors that learn to compress, sample, and pre-process visual information before it is converted to digital form. The results included a fabricated prototype chip, an energy-efficient eye-tracking camera, and a camera design that protects personal privacy at the hardware level. We extended these ideas to implantable heart devices, cutting power to a small fraction of conventional approaches without sacrificing detection accuracy.

A curiosity-driven exploration also led to an unexpected discovery. Concepts from an area of physics known as parity-time symmetry can be integrated onto standard chips, overcoming long-standing performance limits of electronic oscillators. This finding was published in Nature Nanotechnology.

Altogether, the project produced more than 30 peer-reviewed publications at leading venues in chip design, computer architecture, machine learning, and computer vision. These include a Best Paper Award at the top electronic design automation conference and a Spotlight selection at the International Conference on Learning Representations.

Broader Impacts

The project trained ten doctoral students, several undergraduate researchers, and one postdoctoral scholar. Multiple doctoral students completed their degrees, and one former student is now a faculty member at another university. Undergraduate participants gained hands-on research experience, and one continued into doctoral study within the group.

The project also reshaped engineering education. At Washington University in St. Louis, it led to a two-course sequence on hardware for machine learning. At Northeastern University, it led to new graduate courses on deep learning and on the co-design of visual sensors and computing, including material on generative AI for hardware design.

To lower barriers for other researchers, we openly released software tools and large datasets. These include thousands of real-world analog circuit designs, millions of simulated circuit performance records, and a benchmark for testing AI models' understanding of circuits.

The project yielded one granted U.S. patent, additional patent filings, and invention disclosures toward future patents. Collaborations with industry partners helped move these ideas toward practice.

By making electronics more energy-efficient and making circuit design faster and more accessible, this work supports more sustainable AI, longer-lasting mobile and medical devices, and a stronger U.S. semiconductor design workforce.
